Question:
Which fault log included the most number of faulty parts? List the fault log id, description and record time.
answer: SELECT T1.fault_log_entry_id ,  T1.fault_description ,  T1.fault_log_entry_datetime FROM Fault_Log AS T1 JOIN Fault_Log_Parts AS T2 ON T1.fault_log_entry_id  =  T2.fault_log_entry_id GROUP BY T1.fault_log_entry_id ORDER BY count(*) DESC LIMIT 1

prefix_hints.hint_1: Start from the fault log records so the result can include each entry's identifier, description, and recorded datetime: `FROM Fault_Log AS T1`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Link each fault log to its associated faulty-part rows using the shared fault log entry identifier: `JOIN Fault_Log_Parts AS T2 ON T1.fault_log_entry_id = T2.fault_log_entry_id`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Group the joined rows by fault log entry so that the number of associated rows can be counted for each log: `GROUP BY T1.fault_log_entry_id`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Rank the grouped fault logs by their faulty-part counts from highest to lowest and retain the top entry: `ORDER BY count(*) DESC LIMIT 1`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Project the requested identifier, description, and record time for the highest-ranked fault log: `SELECT T1.fault_log_entry_id, T1.fault_description, T1.fault_log_entry_datetime`.

Question:
Find the name of tracks which are in both Movies and music playlists.
answer: SELECT T1.name FROM tracks AS T1 JOIN playlist_tracks AS T2 ON T1.id  =  T2.track_id JOIN playlists AS T3 ON T2.playlist_id  =  T3.id WHERE T3.name  =  'Movies' INTERSECT SELECT T1.name FROM tracks AS T1 JOIN playlist_tracks AS T2 ON T1.id  =  T2.track_id JOIN playlists AS T3 ON T2.playlist_id  =  T3.id WHERE T3.name  =  'Music'

prefix_hints.hint_1: Link each track to its playlist membership through `playlist_tracks` using the track identifier: `FROM tracks AS T1 JOIN playlist_tracks AS T2 ON T1.id = T2.track_id`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Extend the relationship to `playlists` so each matched track can be associated with a playlist name: `JOIN playlists AS T3 ON T2.playlist_id = T3.id`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Build the first result set by projecting track names and restricting membership to the Movies playlist: `SELECT T1.name FROM tracks AS T1 JOIN playlist_tracks AS T2 ON T1.id = T2.track_id JOIN playlists AS T3 ON T2.playlist_id = T3.id WHERE T3.name = 'Movies'`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Build the second result set with the same joins, this time selecting tracks belonging to the Music playlist: `SELECT T1.name FROM tracks AS T1 JOIN playlist_tracks AS T2 ON T1.id = T2.track_id JOIN playlists AS T3 ON T2.playlist_id = T3.id WHERE T3.name = 'Music'`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Return only names occurring in both result sets by placing the set-intersection operator between the Movies and Music SELECT statements: `<Movies SELECT> INTERSECT <Music SELECT>`.

answer: SELECT T1.name FROM tracks AS T1 JOIN playlist_tracks AS T2 ON T1.id = T2.track_id JOIN playlists AS T3 ON T3.id = T2.playlist_id WHERE T3.name = "Movies";

prefix_hints.hint_1: Start from `tracks`, since this table contains the track names that must be returned: `FROM tracks AS T1`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Connect each track to its playlist membership record using the shared track identifier: `JOIN playlist_tracks AS T2 ON T1.id = T2.track_id`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Link each membership record to its playlist so its name can be checked: `JOIN playlists AS T3 ON T3.id = T2.playlist_id`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Restrict the joined records to the playlist named Movies: `WHERE T3.name = "Movies"`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Project the name of every matching track by placing this clause at the beginning of the assembled query: `SELECT T1.name`.

answer: SELECT DISTINCT T1.name FROM races AS T1 JOIN circuits AS T2 ON T1.circuitid = T2.circuitid WHERE T2.country = "Spain" AND T1.year > 2000

prefix_hints.hint_1: Start from the race records because the requested names and years are stored in `races`: `FROM races AS T1`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Join each race to its circuit using their shared circuit identifier so the circuit country becomes available: `JOIN circuits AS T2 ON T1.circuitid = T2.circuitid`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Restrict the joined records to circuits located in Spain: `WHERE T2.country = "Spain"`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Add the strict year condition to retain races held after, rather than during, 2000: `AND T1.year > 2000`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Project the race name and remove duplicates because the same race name may appear in multiple years: `SELECT DISTINCT T1.name`.

prefix_hints.hint_4: Add the inclusive upper date boundary so that qualifying orders extend through January 1, 2010: `AND T2.date_order_placed <= "2010-01-01"`.

prefix_hints.hint_3: Restrict the joined records to the specified team name: `WHERE T2.name = 'Boston Red Stockings'`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Limit the home-game records to the inclusive period from 1990 through 2000: `AND T1.year BETWEEN 1990 AND 2000`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Return the total number of games across all qualifying records by applying `sum` to the home-game count: `SELECT sum(T1.games)`.

Question:
Which staff handled least number of payments? List the full name and the id.
answer: SELECT T1.first_name ,  T1.last_name ,  T1.staff_id FROM staff AS T1 JOIN payment AS T2 ON T1.staff_id  =  T2.staff_id GROUP BY T1.staff_id ORDER BY count(*) ASC LIMIT 1

prefix_hints.hint_1: Start from the staff records and assign the alias used for staff columns: `FROM staff AS T1`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Link each staff member to the payments they handled through the shared `staff_id`: `JOIN payment AS T2 ON T1.staff_id = T2.staff_id`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Group the joined payment rows by staff member so that each staff member's payments can be counted: `GROUP BY T1.staff_id`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Sort the staff groups by their payment count in ascending order, then retain the group with the smallest count: `ORDER BY count(*) ASC LIMIT 1`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Project the selected staff member's first name, last name, and identifier: `SELECT T1.first_name, T1.last_name, T1.staff_id`.

answer: SELECT T1.name_first ,  T1.name_last ,  T2.player_id FROM player AS T1 JOIN manager_award AS T2 ON T1.player_id  =  T2.player_id GROUP BY T2.player_id ORDER BY count(*) DESC LIMIT 1;

Question:
In 2014, what are the id and rank of the team that has the largest average number of attendance?
answer: SELECT T2.team_id ,  T2.rank FROM home_game AS T1 JOIN team AS T2 ON T1.team_id  =  T2.team_id WHERE T1.year  =  2014 GROUP BY T1.team_id ORDER BY avg(T1.attendance) DESC LIMIT 1;

prefix_hints.hint_1: Link home-game attendance records to team records through the shared team identifier so the result can include the team’s rank: `FROM home_game AS T1 JOIN team AS T2 ON T1.team_id = T2.team_id`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Restrict the attendance records to the requested 2014 season: `WHERE T1.year = 2014`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Group the matching home-game rows by team so an average attendance can be calculated for each team: `GROUP BY T1.team_id`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Sort the team groups from the largest average attendance to the smallest: `ORDER BY avg(T1.attendance) DESC`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Project the winning team’s identifier and rank, then retain only the top-ranked attendance group using `SELECT T2.team_id , T2.rank` and `LIMIT 1`.

answer: SELECT T2.address_id ,  T1.city FROM Addresses AS T1 JOIN Student_Addresses AS T2 ON T1.address_id  =  T2.address_id GROUP BY T2.address_id ORDER BY AVG(monthly_rental) DESC LIMIT 1

Question:
Which 3 players won the most player awards? List their full name and id.
answer: SELECT T1.name_first ,  T1.name_last ,  T1.player_id FROM player AS T1 JOIN player_award AS T2 ON T1.player_id  =  T2.player_id GROUP BY T1.player_id ORDER BY count(*) DESC LIMIT 3;

prefix_hints.hint_1: Start from the player records so the result can include each winner's name and identifier: `FROM player AS T1`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Link each player to their award records using the shared player identifier: `JOIN player_award AS T2 ON T1.player_id = T2.player_id`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Group the joined award rows by player so each group represents all awards won by one player: `GROUP BY T1.player_id`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Rank players by their number of award records in descending order and retain only the top three: `ORDER BY count(*) DESC LIMIT 3`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Project the first name, last name, and ID for each of the three qualifying players: `SELECT T1.name_first, T1.name_last, T1.player_id`.

Question:
List players' first name and last name who received salary from team Washington Nationals in both 2005 and 2007.
answer: SELECT T2.name_first ,  T2.name_last FROM salary AS T1 JOIN player AS T2 ON T1.player_id = T2.player_id JOIN team AS T3 ON T3.team_id_br = T1.team_id WHERE T1.year = 2005 AND T3.name = 'Washington Nationals' INTERSECT SELECT T2.name_first , T2.name_last FROM salary AS T1 JOIN player AS T2 ON T1.player_id = T2.player_id JOIN team AS T3 ON T3.team_id_br = T1.team_id WHERE T1.year = 2007 AND T3.name = 'Washington Nationals'

prefix_hints.hint_1: Build the first year-specific result by joining salary records to player names and matching the salary team identifier to the team’s Baseball-Reference identifier: `FROM salary AS T1 JOIN player AS T2 ON T1.player_id = T2.player_id JOIN team AS T3 ON T3.team_id_br = T1.team_id`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Restrict the first result set to Washington Nationals salary records from 2005: `WHERE T1.year = 2005 AND T3.name = 'Washington Nationals'`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Project the player’s first and last names for the 2005 result set: `SELECT T2.name_first , T2.name_last`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Start a second result set with the same name projection and join path, using `INTERSECT` so only names appearing in both years remain: `INTERSECT SELECT T2.name_first , T2.name_last FROM salary AS T1 JOIN player AS T2 ON T1.player_id = T2.player_id JOIN team AS T3 ON T3.team_id_br = T1.team_id`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Complete the second result set by restricting it to Washington Nationals salary records from 2007: `WHERE T1.year = 2007 AND T3.name = 'Washington Nationals'`.

Question:
what is the full name and id of the college with the largest number of baseball players?
answer: SELECT T1.name_full ,  T1.college_id FROM college AS T1 JOIN player_college AS T2 ON T1.college_id  =  T2.college_id GROUP BY T1.college_id ORDER BY count(*) DESC LIMIT 1;

prefix_hints.hint_1: Start from the college records and connect each college to its associated baseball players through the shared college identifier: `FROM college AS T1 JOIN player_college AS T2 ON T1.college_id = T2.college_id`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Group the joined records by college so that each college's linked player records can be counted together: `GROUP BY T1.college_id`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Rank the college groups by their number of joined player records, placing the largest count first: `ORDER BY count(*) DESC`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Keep only the first ranked college, which is the one with the largest number of baseball players: `LIMIT 1`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Return that college's full name and identifier in the projection: `SELECT T1.name_full, T1.college_id`.

Question:
How many players were in the team Boston Red Stockings in 2000?
answer: SELECT count(*) FROM salary AS T1 JOIN team AS T2 ON T1.team_id  =  T2.team_id_br WHERE T2.name  = 'Boston Red Stockings' AND T1.year  =  2000

prefix_hints.hint_1: Start from the salary records, where each row identifies a paid player and their team for a season: `FROM salary AS T1`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Join the team data so the salary team identifier can be matched to the team’s Baseball Reference identifier: `JOIN team AS T2 ON T1.team_id = T2.team_id_br`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Restrict the joined records to the team named Boston Red Stockings: `WHERE T2.name = 'Boston Red Stockings'`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Further restrict the salary records to the requested 2000 season: `AND T1.year = 2000`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Count all rows that remain after applying the join and both filters by using the aggregate projection: `SELECT count(*)`.

Question:

answer: SELECT T2.dept_name ,  T2.dept_address ,  count(*) FROM student AS T1 JOIN department AS T2 ON T1.dept_code  =  T2.dept_code GROUP BY T1.dept_code ORDER BY count(*) DESC LIMIT 3

prefix_hints.hint_1: Start from the student records and join each student to the corresponding department through the shared department code: `FROM student AS T1 JOIN department AS T2 ON T1.dept_code = T2.dept_code`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Group the joined rows by department so that each department produces one aggregate result: `GROUP BY T1.dept_code`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Count the student rows within each department group to obtain its number of students: `count(*)`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Rank departments from the largest student count to the smallest and retain only the top three: `ORDER BY count(*) DESC LIMIT 3`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Project each qualifying department's name, address, and aggregated student count: `SELECT T2.dept_name, T2.dept_address, count(*)`.

Question:
For all directors who directed more than one movie, return the titles of all movies directed by them, along with the director name. Sort by director name, then movie title.

prefix_hints.hint_2: Self-join a second instance of `Movie` so each movie can be matched with another movie by the same director: `JOIN Movie AS T2 ON T1.director = T2.director`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Require the matched rows to have different titles, which identifies directors associated with more than one movie: `WHERE T1.title != T2.title`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Return each qualifying movie title together with its director name: `SELECT T1.title, T1.director`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Sort the resulting rows first by director name and then by movie title: `ORDER BY T1.director, T1.title`.

prefix_hints.hint_3: Connect the patient to their prescription records using the same patient SSN: `JOIN Prescribes AS T3 ON T3.Patient = T2.SSN`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Join each prescription to its medication so the medication name becomes available, then restrict the stays to room 111: `JOIN Medication AS T4 ON T3.Medication = T4.Code WHERE room = 111`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Project the medication name from the joined `Medication` table as the requested result: `SELECT T4.name`.

prefix_hints.hint_3: Join each game to its recorded injury accidents through the game identifier: `JOIN injury_accident AS T3 ON T1.id = T3.game_id`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Keep records where the injury is either Foot injury or Knee problem: `WHERE T3.injury = 'Foot injury' OR T3.injury = 'Knee problem'`.

prefix_hints.hint_3: Count the joined rows within each album group to determine its number of tracks: `count(T1.id)`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Keep only album groups whose track count is greater than 10: `HAVING count(T1.id) > 10`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Return the title of every album that satisfies the grouped count condition by using the projection: `SELECT T1.title`.

prefix_hints.hint_3: Restrict the home-game records to the requested season: `WHERE T1.year = 1907`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Add the park-name condition to retain only records for Columbia Park: `AND T2.park_name = 'Columbia Park'`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Count all rows that satisfy the joined park and year conditions by using the aggregate projection: `SELECT count(*)`.

Question:
Find the subject ID, name of subject and the corresponding number of courses for each subject, and sort by the course count in ascending order.
answer: SELECT T1.subject_id ,  T2.subject_name ,  COUNT(*) FROM Courses AS T1 JOIN Subjects AS T2 ON T1.subject_id  =  T2.subject_id GROUP BY T1.subject_id ORDER BY COUNT(*) ASC

prefix_hints.hint_1: Start from the courses table, since each row represents a course to be counted, and assign it the target alias: `FROM Courses AS T1`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Join each course to its subject record through their shared subject identifier so the subject name is available: `JOIN Subjects AS T2 ON T1.subject_id = T2.subject_id`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Create one result group for each subject so the aggregate is calculated separately per subject: `GROUP BY T1.subject_id`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Count the course rows in each subject group and project the subject ID, subject name, and count: `SELECT T1.subject_id, T2.subject_name, COUNT(*)`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Sort the grouped results from the smallest course count to the largest: `ORDER BY COUNT(*) ASC`.

Question:
What are the name and id of the team offering the lowest average salary?
answer: SELECT T1.name ,  T1.team_id FROM team AS T1 JOIN salary AS T2 ON T1.team_id = T2.team_id GROUP BY T1.team_id ORDER BY avg(T2.salary) ASC LIMIT 1;

prefix_hints.hint_1: Start with the `team` table, which contains the requested team name and identifier: `FROM team AS T1`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Link each team to its salary records using the shared `team_id`: `JOIN salary AS T2 ON T1.team_id = T2.team_id`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Create one result group per team so its salary records can be averaged together: `GROUP BY T1.team_id`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Sort the team groups by average salary from lowest to highest and retain only the first one: `ORDER BY avg(T2.salary) ASC LIMIT 1`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Return both the name and ID of the lowest-average-salary team with the projection: `SELECT T1.name ,  T1.team_id`.

answer: SELECT T1.name_first ,  T1.name_last ,  T1.player_id FROM player AS T1 JOIN player_award AS T2 ON T1.player_id  =  T2.player_id GROUP BY T1.player_id ORDER BY count(*) DESC LIMIT 3;

prefix_hints.hint_3: Combine all award rows belonging to the same player so each player's awards can be counted: `GROUP BY T1.player_id`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Rank players by their number of award records in descending order and retain the top three: `ORDER BY count(*) DESC LIMIT 3`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Project the full name components and player ID for the three qualifying players: `SELECT T1.name_first, T1.name_last, T1.player_id`.

Question:

answer: SELECT T1.title ,  T1.film_id FROM film AS T1 JOIN inventory AS T2 ON T1.film_id  =  T2.film_id GROUP BY T1.film_id ORDER BY count(*) DESC LIMIT 1

prefix_hints.hint_1: Start from the film records and link each film to its physical inventory copies using the shared film identifier: `FROM film AS T1 JOIN inventory AS T2 ON T1.film_id = T2.film_id`.

prefix_hints.hint_3: Measure the number of inventory copies in each film group with the aggregate expression: `count(*)`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Rank films from the greatest copy count to the smallest, then retain only the top-ranked film: `ORDER BY count(*) DESC LIMIT 1`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Project both requested attributes for the winning film—the title followed by its identifier: `SELECT T1.title, T1.film_id`.

prefix_hints.hint_2: Find the earliest date among those cancelled orders, which provides the comparison threshold: `SELECT min(order_date) FROM Customer_Orders WHERE order_status_code = "Cancelled"`.

intermediate_turns.sql: SELECT count ( * )  FROM routes AS T1 JOIN airports AS T2 ON T1.dst_apid   =   T2.apid WHERE T2.country   =   'Italy'

intermediate_turns.question: Can you please tell me the number of routes with the destination airport in Italy operated by the airline with the name 'American Airlines'?
intermediate_turns.sql: SELECT count ( * )  FROM routes AS T1 JOIN airports AS T2 ON T1.dst_apid   =   T2.apid JOIN airlines AS T3 ON T1.alid   =   T3.alid WHERE T2.country   =   'Italy' AND T3.name   =   'American Airlines'

intermediate_turns.question: What are the source airports of those routes?
intermediate_turns.sql: SELECT t1.src_ap FROM routes AS T1 JOIN airports AS T2 ON T1.dst_apid   =   T2.apid JOIN airlines AS T3 ON T1.alid   =   T3.alid WHERE T2.country   =   'Italy' AND T3.name   =   'American Airlines'

Question:
what are name and phone number of patients who had more than one appointment?
answer: SELECT name ,  phone FROM appointment AS T1 JOIN patient AS T2 ON T1.patient  =  T2.ssn GROUP BY T1.patient HAVING count(*)  >  1

prefix_hints.hint_1: Start from the appointment records, since each row represents an appointment that must be counted: `FROM appointment AS T1`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Join each appointment to its patient by matching the appointment’s patient identifier with the patient’s SSN: `JOIN patient AS T2 ON T1.patient = T2.ssn`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Create one group for each patient so that appointments are counted separately per patient: `GROUP BY T1.patient`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Keep only patient groups containing more than one appointment: `HAVING count(*) > 1`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Project the qualifying patients’ names and phone numbers from the patient table: `SELECT name, phone`.

Question:
What is the id and name of the department store that has both marketing and managing department?
answer: SELECT T2.dept_store_id ,  T2.store_name FROM departments AS T1 JOIN department_stores AS T2 ON T1.dept_store_id  =  T2.dept_store_id WHERE T1.department_name  =  "marketing" INTERSECT SELECT T2.dept_store_id ,  T2.store_name FROM departments AS T1 JOIN department_stores AS T2 ON T1.dept_store_id  =  T2.dept_store_id WHERE T1.department_name  =  "managing"

prefix_hints.hint_1: Link each department to its department store using the shared store identifier: `FROM departments AS T1 JOIN department_stores AS T2 ON T1.dept_store_id = T2.dept_store_id`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Build the first result set by retaining stores that contain a marketing department: `WHERE T1.department_name = "marketing"`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Project both the store ID and store name for that first result set: `SELECT T2.dept_store_id, T2.store_name`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Create the second result set with the same join and projection, but filter it to the managing department: `SELECT T2.dept_store_id, T2.store_name FROM departments AS T1 JOIN department_stores AS T2 ON T1.dept_store_id = T2.dept_store_id WHERE T1.department_name = "managing"`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Place `INTERSECT` between the marketing and managing result sets so only identical store ID/name pairs occurring in both are returned: `... WHERE T1.department_name = "marketing" INTERSECT SELECT T2.dept_store_id, T2.store_name ...`.

Question:
What is the latitude, longitude, city of the station from which the shortest trip started?
answer: SELECT T1.lat ,  T1.long ,  T1.city FROM station AS T1 JOIN trip AS T2 ON T1.id  =  T2.start_station_id ORDER BY T2.duration LIMIT 1

prefix_hints.hint_1: Start with the `station` table because it contains the latitude, longitude, and city to be returned: `FROM station AS T1`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Link each station to trips that started there by matching the station ID to the trip's starting-station ID: `JOIN trip AS T2 ON T1.id = T2.start_station_id`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Sort the matched trips by duration in ascending order so that the shortest trip appears first: `ORDER BY T2.duration`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Keep only the first row after sorting to isolate the station associated with the shortest trip: `LIMIT 1`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Project the requested location attributes from the matched station record: `SELECT T1.lat, T1.long, T1.city`.

answer: SELECT T2.customer_last_name ,  T1.customer_id ,  T2.phone_number FROM Orders AS T1 JOIN Customers AS T2 ON T1.customer_id  =  T2.customer_id GROUP BY T1.customer_id ORDER BY count(*) DESC LIMIT 1

prefix_hints.hint_3: Restrict the joined records to the team named Boston Red Stockings: `WHERE T2.name = 'Boston Red Stockings'`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Add the requested inclusive year range so attendance is counted from 2000 through 2010: `AND T1.year BETWEEN 2000 AND 2010`.

answer: SELECT T1.cust_name FROM customer AS T1 JOIN loan AS T2 ON T1.cust_id  =  T2.cust_id WHERE loan_type  =  'Mortgages' INTERSECT SELECT T1.cust_name FROM customer AS T1 JOIN loan AS T2 ON T1.cust_id  =  T2.cust_id WHERE loan_type  =  'Auto'

Question:
What is the total home game attendance of team Boston Red Stockings from 2000 to 2010?
answer: SELECT sum(T1.attendance) FROM home_game AS T1 JOIN team AS T2 ON T1.team_id  =  T2.team_id_br WHERE T2.name  =  'Boston Red Stockings' AND T1.year BETWEEN 2000 AND 2010;

prefix_hints.hint_1: Use `home_game` as the source of attendance records and assign it the target alias: `FROM home_game AS T1`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Join each home-game record to its corresponding team through the identifier used by the target query: `JOIN team AS T2 ON T1.team_id = T2.team_id_br`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Restrict the joined records to the requested team by matching its full name: `WHERE T2.name = 'Boston Red Stockings'`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Add the inclusive year range so that only attendance from 2000 through 2010 is counted: `AND T1.year BETWEEN 2000 AND 2010`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Calculate the total attendance across all qualifying home-game records with the aggregate projection: `SELECT sum(T1.attendance)`.

intermediate_turns.sql: SELECT T1.Name FROM people AS T1 JOIN perpetrator AS T2 ON T1.People_ID   =   T2.People_ID WHERE T2.Country ! =  "China"

intermediate_turns.question: Great - I forgot to ask, can you please show which countries each of the listed perpetrators are associated with?
intermediate_turns.sql: SELECT T1.Name, T2.Country FROM people AS T1 JOIN perpetrator AS T2 ON T1.People_ID   =   T2.People_ID WHERE T2.Country ! =  "China"

intermediate_turns.question: Fantastic - what was the total number of perpetrators in China?
intermediate_turns.sql: SELECT count ( * )  FROM people AS T1 JOIN perpetrator AS T2 ON T1.People_ID  =  T2.People_ID WHERE T2.Country  =  "China"

prefix_hints.hint_3: Create the second result set using the same title projection from the `course` table: `SELECT title FROM course`.

prefix_hints.hint_5: Place the set-difference operator between the Statistics and Psychology result sets so titles appearing in the latter are removed from the former: `EXCEPT`.

Question:
Show the residences that have both a player of gender "M" and a player of gender "F".
answer: SELECT Residence FROM player WHERE gender  =  "M" INTERSECT SELECT Residence FROM player WHERE gender  =  "F"

prefix_hints.hint_1: Build the first branch by identifying male players with the gender condition: `WHERE gender = "M"`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Project the residences from the male-player subset: `SELECT Residence FROM player WHERE gender = "M"`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Build the second branch by identifying female players with the corresponding condition: `WHERE gender = "F"`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Project the residences from the female-player subset: `SELECT Residence FROM player WHERE gender = "F"`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Place the set-intersection operator between the male-residence and female-residence SELECT branches so that only residences appearing in both are returned: `INTERSECT`.

Question:
Show the name of the shop that has the most kind of devices in stock.
answer: SELECT T2.Shop_Name FROM stock AS T1 JOIN shop AS T2 ON T1.Shop_ID  =  T2.Shop_ID GROUP BY T1.Shop_ID ORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC LIMIT 1

prefix_hints.hint_1: Start from `stock`, where each row represents a device kind stocked by a shop: `FROM stock AS T1`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Join the shop information so each stock record can be associated with its shop name: `JOIN shop AS T2 ON T1.Shop_ID = T2.Shop_ID`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Group the stock rows by shop so the number of rows can be counted separately for each shop: `GROUP BY T1.Shop_ID`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Rank shops by their number of stocked device kinds from highest to lowest: `ORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Return the name of the top-ranked shop by combining the projection and one-row limit around the preceding clauses: `SELECT T2.Shop_Name` and `LIMIT 1`.

Question:
Find Alice's friends of friends.
answer: SELECT DISTINCT T4.name FROM PersonFriend AS T1 JOIN Person AS T2 ON T1.name  =  T2.name JOIN PersonFriend AS T3 ON T1.friend  =  T3.name JOIN PersonFriend AS T4 ON T3.friend  =  T4.name WHERE T2.name  =  'Alice' AND T4.name != 'Alice'

prefix_hints.hint_1: Start from Alice’s direct friendship records and link each record to the corresponding person by name: `FROM PersonFriend AS T1 JOIN Person AS T2 ON T1.name = T2.name`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Follow each direct friend into another friendship record, treating `T1.friend` as the person whose friends must be found: `JOIN PersonFriend AS T3 ON T1.friend = T3.name`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Continue the relationship path to the friends-of-friends records using the second friendship’s `friend` value: `JOIN PersonFriend AS T4 ON T3.friend = T4.name`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Restrict the starting person to Alice and exclude Alice herself from the resulting names: `WHERE T2.name = 'Alice' AND T4.name != 'Alice'`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Project the resulting names and remove duplicates that can arise through multiple friendship paths: `SELECT DISTINCT T4.name`.

metadata.question: Find Alice's friends of friends.

intermediate_turns.question: Can you please tell me who the friends of Alice's friends are?
intermediate_turns.sql: SELECT DISTINCT T4.name FROM PersonFriend AS T1 JOIN Person AS T2 ON T1.name   =   T2.name JOIN PersonFriend AS T3 ON T1.friend   =   T3.name JOIN PersonFriend AS T4 ON T3.friend   =   T4.name WHERE T2.name   =   'Alice' AND T4.name ! =  'Alice'

Question:
Show the station name with greatest number of trains.
answer: SELECT T2.name FROM train_station AS T1 JOIN station AS T2 ON T1.station_id  =  T2.station_id GROUP BY T1.station_id ORDER BY count(*) DESC LIMIT 1

prefix_hints.hint_1: Start from the station-to-train association table, where each row represents a train assigned to a station: `FROM train_station AS T1`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Join the station table to obtain each associated station's name using the shared station identifier: `JOIN station AS T2 ON T1.station_id = T2.station_id`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Group the joined rows by station so that the number of association rows can be counted for each station: `GROUP BY T1.station_id`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Rank stations by their train count from greatest to least and retain only the top station: `ORDER BY count(*) DESC LIMIT 1`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Project the name of the highest-ranked station in the SELECT clause: `SELECT T2.name`.

Question:
What is the title and credits of the course that is taught in the largest classroom (with the highest capacity)?
answer: SELECT T3.title ,  T3.credits FROM classroom AS T1 JOIN SECTION AS T2 ON T1.building  =  T2.building AND T1.room_number  =  T2.room_number JOIN course AS T3 ON T2.course_id  =  T3.course_id WHERE T1.capacity  =  (SELECT max(capacity) FROM classroom)

prefix_hints.hint_1: Compute the highest classroom capacity as a scalar benchmark using an aggregate subquery: `SELECT max(capacity) FROM classroom`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Start from classrooms and connect each one to the sections held there by matching both its building and room number: `FROM classroom AS T1 JOIN SECTION AS T2 ON T1.building = T2.building AND T1.room_number = T2.room_number`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Join each matched section to its course record so that the course title and credits become available: `JOIN course AS T3 ON T2.course_id = T3.course_id`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Keep only sections taught in a classroom whose capacity equals the maximum capacity calculated by the subquery: `WHERE T1.capacity = (SELECT max(capacity) FROM classroom)`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Project the requested title and credit value from the matched course record: `SELECT T3.title, T3.credits`.

Question:
What are the name and id of the team with the most victories in 2008 postseason?
answer: SELECT T2.name ,  T1.team_id_winner FROM postseason AS T1 JOIN team AS T2 ON T1.team_id_winner  =  T2.team_id_br WHERE T1.year  =  2008 GROUP BY T1.team_id_winner ORDER BY count(*) DESC LIMIT 1;

prefix_hints.hint_1: Start from the postseason records, where each series identifies its winning team: `FROM postseason AS T1`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Join each postseason winner to the team table using the winner ID and the team’s Baseball-Reference ID so its name is available: `JOIN team AS T2 ON T1.team_id_winner = T2.team_id_br`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Restrict the postseason series to those played in 2008: `WHERE T1.year = 2008`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Group the series by winning team, rank teams by their number of victories, and keep the highest-ranked one: `GROUP BY T1.team_id_winner ORDER BY count(*) DESC LIMIT 1`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Project the winning team’s name and postseason winner ID in the requested order: `SELECT T2.name, T1.team_id_winner`.

Question:
Find the names of customers who either have an deputy policy or uniformed policy.
answer: SELECT DISTINCT t2.customer_details FROM policies AS t1 JOIN customers AS t2 ON t1.customer_id  =  t2.customer_id WHERE t1.policy_type_code  =  "Deputy" OR t1.policy_type_code  =  "Uniform"

prefix_hints.hint_1: Start with the `policies` table because it contains the policy type used to identify qualifying customers: `FROM policies AS t1`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Link each policy to its customer through the shared customer identifier: `JOIN customers AS t2 ON t1.customer_id = t2.customer_id`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Include customers whose policy type is Deputy by applying the first filter condition: `WHERE t1.policy_type_code = "Deputy"`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Extend the filter to also include customers whose policy type is Uniform: `OR t1.policy_type_code = "Uniform"`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Return each qualifying customer's details only once, since a customer may have multiple matching policies: `SELECT DISTINCT t2.customer_details`.

Question:

answer: SELECT T1.campus ,  sum(T2.degrees) FROM campuses AS T1 JOIN degrees AS T2 ON T1.id  =  T2.campus WHERE T1.county  =  "Orange" AND T2.year  >=  2000 GROUP BY T1.campus

prefix_hints.hint_1: Link each campus record to its degree records using the campus identifier: `FROM campuses AS T1 JOIN degrees AS T2 ON T1.id = T2.campus`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Restrict the joined records to campuses located in Orange county: `WHERE T1.county = "Orange"`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Add the year condition so that only degrees granted from 2000 onward are included: `AND T2.year >= 2000`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Create one result group for each campus so its qualifying degree counts can be aggregated: `GROUP BY T1.campus`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Project each campus name and sum the degrees granted across its qualifying yearly records: `SELECT T1.campus, sum(T2.degrees)`.

Question:
Which customer, who has made at least one payment, has spent the least money? List his or her first name, last name, and the id.
answer: SELECT T1.first_name ,  T1.last_name ,  T1.customer_id FROM customer AS T1 JOIN payment AS T2 ON T1.customer_id  =  T2.customer_id GROUP BY T1.customer_id ORDER BY sum(amount) ASC LIMIT 1

prefix_hints.hint_1: Start with customers and link them to their payment records using the shared customer identifier; this naturally limits the candidates to customers who made at least one payment: `FROM customer AS T1 JOIN payment AS T2 ON T1.customer_id = T2.customer_id`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Combine each customer's payment rows so their total spending can be evaluated as one group: `GROUP BY T1.customer_id`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Calculate each grouped customer's total spending using the payment amount column: `sum(amount)`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Sort the customer groups from the smallest total spend to the largest and retain only the first one: `ORDER BY sum(amount) ASC LIMIT 1`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Return the least-spending customer's requested first name, last name, and ID in the projection: `SELECT T1.first_name, T1.last_name, T1.customer_id`.

Question:
Find the name of the department that has the fewest members.
answer: SELECT T1.DName FROM DEPARTMENT AS T1 JOIN MEMBER_OF AS T2 ON T1.DNO  =  T2.DNO GROUP BY T2.DNO ORDER BY count(*) ASC LIMIT 1

prefix_hints.hint_1: Start from departments so the department name is available for the result: `FROM DEPARTMENT AS T1`.
prefix_hints.hint_2: Link each department to its membership records using the shared department number: `JOIN MEMBER_OF AS T2 ON T1.DNO = T2.DNO`.
prefix_hints.hint_3: Group the joined membership records by department so each department's rows can be counted together: `GROUP BY T2.DNO`.
prefix_hints.hint_4: Sort the department groups from the fewest membership rows to the most and retain only the first group: `ORDER BY count(*) ASC LIMIT 1`.
prefix_hints.hint_5: Project the name of the department selected by the grouping, ordering, and limit clauses: `SELECT T1.DName`.
